cognate: kin terms *ph₂tḗr, *méh₂tēr, *swésōr exact in both; the 'slay' element *gʷʰen- is in the Vedic compounds (-hán-) and survives in Norse in the parallel compounds fǫðurbani/bróðurbani (bani < *gʷʰon-), Greek πατροφονεύς, Irish guin athar
drift_or_renewal: the Norse law renews the verb with drepa; *gʷʰen- survives in Norse only in the -bani compounds
shared_syntax: a list of 'killer of kin X' items, the same kin terms in the same order (father/mother/sister), naming a class of offender: Vedic yó mātṛhā́ pitṛhā́ svasṛhā́ 'who is a mother-, father-, sister-slayer'; Norse ef maðr drepr fǫður sinn eða ... móður ... eða systur 'if a man kills his father or ... mother ... or sister'
context: both mark the kin-slayer as the worst offender, beyond expiation: AVP lists them among the duṣkṛt- 'evil-doers' whose defilement is wiped off; the Norse law makes him óbótamaðr, a man for whom no compensation exists. The epic has the same 'no expiation for killing a father' idea (MBh 14.80 prāyaścittaṃ na asti / niṣkṛtir na vidyate ... pitaraṃ hatvā)
note: Kin-term + 'slayer' compounds come from a productive type (Ved. vṛtrahán-, Gk ἀνδροφόνος, ON mannbani), and setting kin-slaying apart is close to universal, so the match may have arisen independently. The Greek and Norse -bani/-φονεύς compounds usually mean 'the killer of someone's father' (the target of vengeance), not 'killer of his own father'. Recalled: Lat. parricida and the place of kin-slaying in IE law.
